about: The exchange with which the priest opens the Preface. Cyprian of Carthage quotes it already in the third century: the priest, before the prayer, prepares the minds of the brethren by saying Sursum corda. “Habémus ad Dóminum” has no verb to translate — literally we have towards the Lord; the object left unsaid is the hearts just spoken of. The answer “Dignum et iustum est” is the phrase the priest picks up at once in the first words of the Preface: Vere dignum et iustum est.

s01.narrative: The priest lays his hands on either side of the altar and raises them a little as he says Sursum corda; at Grátias agámus he joins them before his breast and bows his head.

s05.translation: We have them lifted to the Lord.

s06.translation: Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.

w002.function: One written word carrying two: the preposition cum stands after the pronoun, as it always does with the personal pronouns (mecum, tecum, nobíscum).

w006.function: The answer is not “and with you”: it speaks of the priest's spirit, of the gift he received at ordination.

w007.function: The call has no verb — only an adverb of direction and an object. Latin leaves it to be understood what is to be done with the hearts.

w008.function: Accusative, though no verb governs it: the form shows that it is the object of an understood “lift up”.

w009.function: The answer does not repeat the command but states that it has been done; the object (“them”) is again left unsaid.

w012.function: Grátias ágere, to render thanks, is the fixed Latin phrase; from it the Eucharist takes its name, which is Greek for thanksgiving.

w013.function: The subjunctive in the first person plural has the force of an invitation: let us do it.

w015.function: In apposition to “Dómino” (w014), and so in the dative.

w017.function: Neuter with no noun: it is a worthy thing. The priest takes these two words up again in the first sentence of the Preface.
